notes: The SHORT, on the v2 plate kit. Every `plate` here is a registry key and
every `bind` target is a slot that plate DECLARES — the renderer puts the
text in the slot and does nothing else. Type is set in the face, size,
weight and colour role the kit declares for that slot's role, so the
character budgets are the kit's own `maxChars` rather than something
measured by running a fitter over this file.
THE VERTICAL SET IS NOT THE WHOLE KIT. The plates the kit draws 16:9 only
(the peer scatter, the multiple bridge, the flow plates, the dense
timeline and the rest) need horizontal room to be readable and do not
belong in a fifty-second vertical cut. Nothing here reaches for one.
Positions and type sizes are fractions of FRAME HEIGHT, so one template
holds at any delivery resolution. Large type and the caption band never
coexist: a shot carrying type at 6.5% of frame height or more sets
captions false, and the parser refuses the template if it does not.
THE HOST IS IN ONE SHOT, THE TURN, IN CLOSE-UP. He was in the
cold open, the payoff and the close, all three at full figure in a wide
room — which is the shot you use when the room is the point. The turn is
the line the whole cut rests on and it was being told on bare ground with
nobody in it. `host/close-up` is head and shoulders and it exists for
exactly that beat.

A STATIC PLATE MAY HOLD. The ceiling was written when every plate in the kit boiled; some are `playback: static` now, because a figure that moves is a figure being re-read. What keeps a data beat short is the ceiling itself (`short_max_hold_s`, 8 s), which is already more than a fifty-second cut of eight or nine beats gives any one of them.

ALTERNATES: a beat may name other plates that can carry it, and code picks between them, rotating off what the last few videos used. The writer still chooses nothing — that is the point of a format that exists to be mass-produced. An alternate restates `bind` when it names its slots differently, and inherits when it does not.

ORDERS: a shot with an `anchor` starts where its own words are spoken. An unmarked script is one take written to the authored beat order, so it is only offered the orders that keep that sequence. A script whose narration carries [BEAT: key] markers says where each beat starts, and the cut follows its markers, so the orders that move anchored beats are open to it (item 2).

THE ROUND-ONE PHONE PLATES that a short script can fill are alternates here: the fifth hook card, the move on the day in both directions, and the one-line close. Placing a figure the size of the move's on a shot with captions switches the captions off for that shot, in code, because the template's `captions` flag cannot know which plate the rotation will pick.

WIPES MARK A CHANGE OF SUBJECT (item 13): a shot with `enter: wipe` is wiped in, sweep and page alternating, at most three a short; every other cut stays hard. A wipe on every cut would be a signpost on every cut, which is none.

THE CLEAR AREA (item 27). `safe` is the band a phone shows clear of YouTube's own furniture: the title and the buttons over the foot of the frame, the search bar over the head. A card's words are placed inside it: its plate moves or shrinks to fit (no further than 85% for words the beat needs, 94% to keep a caption), an optional line that still falls outside is left off, and the caption band is held inside it too. The manifest's `safe_area` names anything that is not.

THE WORKBOOK FILLS WHAT THE SCRIPT CANNOT (items 1, 3, 4, 5, 23). `data.*` is a card the operator's workbook fills on its own and `news.*` is the release and the wires off its News sheet. A video with no workbook has none of those drawings, and a beat with nothing left it can fill is dropped rather than drawn empty (item 25).

shots.notes: The hook card is the format's own opener — three treatments, and which one a video gets is a property of the script, not of this file. THE TICKER AND THE MOVE IN FRAME ONE (item 6): `move` takes the day's signed move and counts up over the first half second while the hook is spoken; `sub` takes the rest of the summary. A summary that does not lead with a signed move leaves `move` empty and keeps the whole summary in `sub`.

alts.notes: Same three slots, a different treatment.
The third treatment. `huge` goes unfilled, which is the drawing, not a gap.

The fifth treatment: the hook on a full field with the ticker at the foot, so the eye lands on the sentence before the chip. The same slots. `hook-card-t4` is not here on purpose — it leads with the figure at 240pt, and the next beat is that figure.

shots.notes: A REAL PICTURE (item 34). Every frame of a short was drawn type on the dark ground; this is the company itself, a photograph of its stores or its building off the same chain the long searches (cache, Wikimedia Commons, the company's site), in design's media frame. With no picture found the shot is dropped: a frame round "imagery unavailable" is not a picture. The credit goes out with the video's other credits.

The price, as a path through the figures the data carries. `plot-area` is a data region: it takes the series and the renderer draws it, which is not the renderer computing anything — it is being handed one.

alts.notes: THE MOVE AS ONE FIGURE, WITH ITS ARROW. The arrow is drawn, so the plate has to match the sign: `chart.move_up` is the move summary's leading figure only when it opens on a `+`, and nothing otherwise, which makes this plate ineligible on a fall. The rest of the summary is the label. It needs no price data, so a short rendered without prices still has a picture for this beat. The session path the plate reserves room for stays empty: the price data is daily closes, and six of those in a box drawn for one session would read as a day.
The falling twin, eligible only on a move summary that opens on a minus.
WHERE THE PRICE SITS IN ITS YEAR (item 4), off the Snapshot sheet's 52-week high, low and price. The rail is the range; the mark is today.

SHORT INTEREST (item 4), only above 10% of the float, off the Snapshot sheet. Days to cover and the cost to borrow stay empty: the workbook carries no float volume or borrow rate, and an invented one is the thing this channel never prints.

TODAY'S SESSION (item 4), open to close against the prior close, off Yahoo's free five-minute prices. Never synthetic, and withheld when the session's move and the writer's move disagree by more than three points: a chart contradicting the voice is worse than another chart.

shots.notes: A headline on paper, in the band drawn for it. Three treatments exist so two headlines in one video are not the same picture twice.

alts.notes: NEWS-RELEASE ART, AND THE SCRIPT ALREADY CARRIES IT. All three rows are REQUIRED (item 25): a stack of three with an empty row is a broken drawing, so the rotation only reaches for it when the writer filed three headlines.

THE RELEASE ITSELF (item 5). The News sheet row whose headline is this video's news is opened from its link, and the masthead, dateline, headline and first paragraph are the page's own. Taken whenever it can be read: it is this story and no other. A page that refuses a script, or a headline with no row, leaves the rotation to the bands.
THE WIRES (item 5): the News sheet's three latest headlines with their dates, oldest at the top. A headline longer than the strip is cut at its first clause break or skipped, never mid-phrase.
Five wires, for a week when the volume of coverage is the point. Only with five rows that fit.

shots.notes: The line the cut rests on, told to camera in close-up. Allowed to be empty — a video with no turn drops this shot rather than holding an empty frame. The room is a ROLE, not a key: three angles fill `talk` and which one a video gets is its seed's, so the channel's shorts are not all shot from the same chair.

ONE METRIC A CARD (item 26). The sheet set four rows of six figures at 30 px, under captions twice that size, and held it 11 seconds: on a phone it was a table nobody could read, and its empty rows were the "revenue ... net income" frames. Now each row the writer names is a card of its own, coming up as that row is read (`numbers.1` listens for the second row's name): its six years as bars on a scale that starts at zero, the same row as where it started against where it is, or the latest figure at display size with where it came from. The rotation walks the three drawings, so four rows are never one layout four times. The figures are the workbook's History sheet wherever the writer's row names one (item 23); the axis ticks are round numbers on the scale of the printed figures.

alts.notes: Where the row started against where it is, and how far it went: points for a margin, nothing across zero.
The latest figure at display size, with where it came from under it.

shots.notes: What the sheet meant, in the plate drawn for a line worth pulling out. The numbers comment is written at two hundred characters and there is nowhere on a sheet to put one. CAPTIONS OFF (item 8): the card IS the line being said, word for word, so the caption band would print it twice.

alts.notes: The read as a term and its meaning. `definition` names its slots nothing like `quote-pull`, so it restates the binds. No kicker: the sheet's unit ("$M") said nothing over a sentence.

shots.notes: Two things that are both true at once. The plate the format opens on more than any other.

alts.notes: CHEAP OR A TRAP, ANSWERED WITH THE WORKBOOK (item 1): the growth today's price needs (the Valuation sheet's reverse DCF) as one mark on the same scale as what the last four years delivered (free cash flow's and revenue's CAGR). Taken whenever the sheet has them; the two-sided card is the fallback.

meme.notes: The one place for a meme: the tail of the verdict, after the drop and the number have landed and before the close. Never the turn, which is him talking to camera.

shots.notes: The one figure the video is about, at the size it deserves. Item 2: which figure is the writer's `payoff_row`, else the first row, at its latest period.

alts.notes: THE PAYOFF'S OWN NUMBER (item 2). The figure is the row the writer names in `payoff_row`, at its latest period, and its label says which row and which year, so the number the verdict turns on is not simply whatever row came first.

shots.notes: ONE THING AT STATEMENT SIZE, FIRST (item 25). The three-line close drew a conclusion in `line-1` and two empty rules under it, which is the empty furniture the samples were full of. It is an alternate now, and only for a conclusion of exactly three sentences, one a line. The handle sits in the kicker: this plate's date label is in the caption band.

alts.notes: The conclusion as a pulled line.
THREE LINES FOR THREE SENTENCES. `sent.3.i` is sentence i of a conclusion that has exactly three, and nothing otherwise, so this drawing is only in the rotation when every line has one.

orders.name: news-first
orders.notes: Why before how much: the headline straight after the hook, then the chart it moved. Moves two pinned beats, so it is cut only for a script whose markers put `headline` before `move` — the writing prompt names this order before a word is written.

orders.name: turn-after-numbers
orders.notes: The evidence first and the pivot after it: Dennis turns the story once the numbers are on the table, straight into cheap-or-trap. Moves the pinned `turn`, so it is cut only for a script marked in this order.
